newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian referendum exercise could flop amid apathy.
newsitem.headline: Italian referendum exercise could flop amid apathy.

text.p: Italy holds seven referendums on Sunday, including one on privatisation, but the exercise could flop amid apathy, media disinterest and advice to voters from critics to go to the beach instead of the ballot box.

The votes, six of them championed by the minority Radical Party, concern issues as diverse as restrictions on hunting, the career opportunities of magistrates and proposals to abolish Italy's Agriculture Ministry and its journalists' guild.
Under Italian law, more than 50 percent of the eligible electorate of 49 million people has to take part in the individual referendums for the results to be valid.
Potentially the most important issue is a call by the Radical Party for the abolition of the state's right to retain a controlling "golden share" in strategic privatised industries.
The "golden share" option has not been exercised in any privatisation so far but could prove crucial in forthcoming stock offerings in telecoms giant Stet and energy utility ENEL.

Media magnate Silvio Berlusconi's free-market Forza Italia is the only mainstream political party advising supporters to vote to abolish the "golden share" law, a position shared by the powerful industrial employers' federation Confindustria.
Equities analysts, however, said financial markets were not looking closely at the referendum, the fifth national balloting exercise in five years.

"The market is not giving much weight to this because it has largely discounted that the quorum won't be achieved," one trader said. "I'd also like to know how the average voter is meant to understand the question."

Referendums have proved a powerful tool to force legislative change in Italy since the early 1970s, allowing the people to intervene on fundamental concerns that the country's ponderous parliament either cannot or will not tackle effectively.

Opponents of the latest round, however, say the instrument risks being devalued by what the leftist newspaper L'Unita this week called a "Russian salad" of issues, many of them either trivial or beyond the grasp of ordinary voters.
L'Unita, controlled by the largest party in Italy's centre-left government, called for a boycott of the vote.
Other respected figures, including veteran commentator Indro Montanelli, have also weighed it with criticism that the exercise will discredit democracy.
"There are certain issues on which it is right to seek the opinion of citizens. One obvious example is divorce," said Montanelli.
"But can you tell me what sense it makes to decide by universal suffrage whether the Ministry of Agriculture should stay in place?".

The Radical Party, a libertarian movement headed by civil rights campaigner Marco Pannella, has championed the referendum cause and won its greatest victory in 1974 with a vote that legalised civil divorce in Roman Catholic Italy.

It had initially called for 36 separate issues to go to ballot this year, a mountainous total reduced by rejection of most of the requests by the Constitutional Court and changes by parliament in the contested legislation.

Pannella has taken recently to dressing as a ghost, parading in a white sheet on television and through the streets of cities to protest at what he says is a plot by political parties and the media to turn people off voting.
"People are going to be literally afraid to go to polling stations," Pannella alleged on Thursday.
